Differential equation

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis
OurBigBook.com Words: 22k Articles: 330
A differential equation is an equation relating an unknown function to its derivatives. It specifies how change depends on the present state, and sometimes on the independent variables themselves. A solution of a differential equation is a function satisfying that relation throughout a stated domain; giving a formula without its domain can conceal a point where the equation is undefined.
The central idea is to turn a local law into a whole trajectory. For example, y′=ry, with constant r, says that the instantaneous derivative is proportional to the current value. If y(0)=100 and r=0.2 per day, the solution of a differential equation is y(t)=100e0.2t, so y(5)=100e≈271.83. This is an ideal growth model assuming a constant proportional rate; the exponential function emerges from repeatedly applying the same local rule. Changing the sign of r gives exponential decay.
An ordinary differential equation uses one independent variable. A partial differential equation can involve several, such as space and time, and uses partial derivatives. Additional information selects a particular solution of a differential equation: an initial condition describes a starting state, whereas a boundary condition imposes constraints at the edge of a domain. The useful questions extend beyond finding a formula: does a solution of a differential equation exist, is it unique, and what happens to it over time?

Direction field (y′=f(t,y))

Words: 183
Differential equation OurBigBook.com
A direction field for y′=f(t,y) places a short segment with slope f(t,y) at each sampled point where f is defined. A function graph of a solution of a differential equation follows these segments: its tangent line has exactly the prescribed slope. Segment length is a drawing choice, rather than a speed; arrows, if used, point toward increasing t. An isocline collects points with one common slope.
For Newton's law of cooling, y′=−0.1(y−20) with time in minutes and temperature in degrees Celsius, the slopes at y=80,40,20,10 are respectively −6,−2,0,1 degrees Celsius per minute. Each horizontal row is an isocline, because this autonomous differential equation has no explicit time dependence. Above 20 the solutions of a differential equation descend, below 20 they rise, and y=20 is an equilibrium point.
The highlighted initial condition y(0)=80 selects one curve from the family. The picture reveals approach to the equilibrium point before any algebra is done. Under the hypotheses of the Picard-Lindelöf theorem, distinct function graphs of solutions cannot cross or even meet in the time-state plane. A direction field alone does not guarantee uniqueness: several curves can share a tangent line at the same point when those hypotheses fail. See the delayed-start example under initial value problem.
This geometric interpretation is developed in Direction Fields, Isoclines, Integral Curves.

Isocline (f(x,y)=k)

Words: 312
Differential equation OurBigBook.com
For the first-order ordinary differential equation y′=f(x,y) defined on an open subset D of the plane, an isocline of slope k is the level set
{(x,y)∈D:f(x,y)=k}.
(1)
Here k is a constant. At every point of this isocline, the direction field prescribes a tangent vector proportional to (1,k) for a solution of a differential equation. It does not generally prescribe the tangent line of the isocline itself. The level set can have several components or fail to be a smooth curve, and points outside D are excluded.
For example, take y′=x−y on the whole plane. Its isoclines are the parallel straight lines
x−y=k,y=x−k.
(2)
Each line has slope 1, while the direction field along it has slope k. Thus the isocline y=x carries horizontal segments even though the line itself rises. A function graph of a solution of a differential equation follows the segments, rather than following this line. Only the isocline with k=1, namely y=x−1, is also a solution of a differential equation.[ref]
The first-order linear differential equation has the exact family
y(x)=x−1+Ae−x,y′(x)=1−Ae−x=x−y(x).
(3)
The initial condition y(x0​)=y0​ selects A=(y0​−x0​+1)ex0​ and hence a unique solution of a differential equation for every real x. The picture shows y(0)=−1,0,1,2. For A=0 the solution of a differential equation stays on the k=1 isocline; for other A it moves through different isoclines. These formulas check the pictured trajectories by direct differentiation, independently of how the direction field was sampled.
The zero-slope isocline f(x,y)=0 is called a nullcline. Below the nullcline y=x in this example, y′>0; above it, y′<0. For A>0, the solution of a differential equation meets it at x=logA, where y′=0 and y′′=1, a strict local minimum. The nullcline is therefore a useful guide to turning points, although it is not itself a solution of a differential equation. In the equivalent planar autonomous differential equation x˙=1, y˙​=x−y, it is the nullcline for the second component; there is no equilibrium point, because the first component never vanishes.
This makes isoclines useful even when no explicit solution of a differential equation is available: organize a direction field by common slopes, read where function graphs rise or fall, and identify possible turning points on nullclines.

Jump condition

Words: 41
Differential equation OurBigBook.com
A jump condition relates the one-sided limits of a solution or its derivatives across a discontinuity or singular forcing. Integrating a differential equation across a shrinking interval containing a Dirac delta source determines the permitted jump. A jump condition for an impulse and Rankine-Hugoniot condition are specific instances with different governing equations.

Delay differential equation

Words: 22
Differential equation OurBigBook.com
A delay differential equation relates a derivative at the current argument to values at earlier arguments. For example, the Buchstab function obeys dud​(uw(u))=w(u−1) for u>2.

Solution of a differential equation

Words: 56
Differential equation OurBigBook.com
A classical solution is a sufficiently differentiable function that satisfies a differential equation and any prescribed initial or boundary conditions. A weak solution instead satisfies an appropriate integral or distributional identity in a specified function space. For a smooth locally Lipschitz continuous vector field, an ordinary differential equation has a unique local solution for each initial state; this does not by itself ensure global existence or boundedness.

Ordinary differential equation (F(t,y,y′,…,y(n))=0)

Words: 21k Articles: 324
Differential equation OurBigBook.com
An ordinary differential equation relates an unknown function of one independent variable to its ordinary derivatives. Its order is the highest derivative appearing. Thus y′=−k(y−Ta​) is first order, while the harmonic oscillator equation y′′+ω2y=0 is second order. A first-order equation in explicit form is
y′(t)=f(t,y(t)).
(4)
Here t need not be time, and y can be a vector, giving a system of coupled ordinary differential equations. A classical solution of a differential equation is a sufficiently differentiable function on an interval which satisfies the equation at every point. For the explicit first-order equation, if f is continuous, this solution of a differential equation has a continuous derivative.
For Newton's law of cooling, the state is a single temperature; for a second-order differential equation, a first-order system also records its first derivative. This is why a starting position alone does not specify a harmonic oscillator trajectory: its starting velocity matters too.
The power of an ordinary differential equation is that one rule describes a whole family of histories. An initial value problem chooses one history when uniqueness holds. An autonomous differential equation has f independent of t; its equilibrium points satisfy f(y∗​)=0 and give constant solutions of a differential equation. Equations with explicit time dependence can instead respond to a changing environment.

First integral of an ordinary differential equation (It​+∇I⋅f=0)

Words: 75
Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A first integral of y′=f(t,y) is a differentiable function I(t,y) whose value is constant along solutions through every time and state in its domain. The chain rule makes this equivalent to the displayed pointwise identity. For I(y)=yTSy with symmetric S, it becomes yTSf(t,y)=0. This identity at the implicit stage is what proves exact Runge-Kutta conservation of quadratic invariants for the implicit midpoint rule. Invariance asserted only on the image of one initial-time flow needs that image to contain the stage under consideration.

Second-order differential equation (y′′=f(x,y,y′))

Words: 49
Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A second-order ordinary differential equation involves a second derivative as its highest derivative. In explicit form y′′=f(x,y,y′), introducing v=y′ converts it into the first-order system y′=v, v′=f(x,y,v). Under local regularity and Lipschitz continuity in the dependent variables, an initial value problem is specified by both y(x0​) and y′(x0​). The linear case is a second-order linear differential equation.

A first-order ordinary differential equation with complex independent and dependent variables is solved by a holomorphic function on an ordinary domain, and its analytic continuation can have branch points. Painlevé property

Words: 144
Complex ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
The Painlevé property excludes movable critical singularities, such as branch points, of the analytically continued general solution of a complex differential equation. A common stronger formulation requires every movable singularity to be a pole, so local solutions are meromorphic there. Fixed singularities determined by the coefficients are distinguished from movable ones whose locations depend on initial data. Riccati equations with meromorphic coefficients have only movable poles at ordinary points: linearization expresses their solutions as logarithmic derivatives of linear-system solutions. More generally, set w=f/g and solve the holomorphic linear system f′=bf+cg, g′=−af. Its quotient satisfies w′=aw2+bw+c directly. Initial data g(z0​)=1, f(z0​)=w(z0​) recover every local solution, and holomorphic f,g make the quotient a meromorphic function, even at zeros of a. At a zero of g with a=0, uniqueness prevents f=0 there, so g′=−af=0 and the pole is simple. This proves the absence of movable branching without assuming that the quadratic coefficient never vanishes.

Painlevé determinateness theorem

Words: 134
Complex ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
For a first-order ordinary differential equation rational in the dependent variable, with coefficients meromorphic on the chosen independent-variable surface, analytic continuation along an arc ending outside the fixed exceptional set has a definite limit in the Riemann sphere. Its movable singularities are poles or algebraic branch points. To see the limiting assertion, the cluster set of a continuous lifted arc is connected and compact. Any cluster value where the vector field is holomorphic permits uniform local continuation by the Picard-Lindelöf theorem. Otherwise the cluster set lies in finitely many coefficient poles, so it is a singleton. At a pole of the vector field, the inverse equation is holomorphic; its solution has a finite-order critical point, giving a convergent root expansion. The reciprocal dependent variable handles infinity. Points where both reduced numerator and denominator vanish belong to the fixed exceptional set and are excluded from this argument.

A solution has a movable singularity if its location varies with the initial data. For example w′=w2 has solutions w=−1/(z−c), whose pole moves with c. The Painlevé determinateness theorem restricts movable singularities of first-order equations rational in the dependent variable to poles and algebraic branch points.

A singular location is fixed if its position is determined by the coefficients, independently of the initial data. Not every solution must actually be singular there. For a rational first-order equation, coefficient poles and exceptional fibres where the reduced numerator and denominator have common zeros are included among the possible fixed locations.

Implicit solution (F(x,y)=C)

Words: 510
Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
An implicit solution describes a solution of a differential equation through a relation F(x,y)=C, instead of isolating y in an explicit formula. The relation describes a level set; an actual scalar solution of a differential equation must be a differentiable function y(x) on an interval whose function graph lies in the equation's domain. A whole level set need not be one such function graph.
For example, consider
y′=−yx​,D={(x,y):y=0}.
(5)
Implicit differentiation of x2+y2=C gives 2x+2yy′=0. For C>0, the circle contains two solutions of a differential equation,
y+​(x)=C−x2​,y−​(x)=−C−x2​,−C​<x<C​.
(6)
Both satisfy the equation on the stated open interval, and their function graphs stay in D. An initial condition (x0​,y0​)∈D fixes C=x02​+y02​ and selects the sign of y0​. In particular, y(0)=2 gives C=4 and the upper branch on (−2,2). The constant alone does not select the branch.[ref]
The precise local criterion uses the implicit function theorem. Let F be continuously differentiable on an open subset of the plane, with F(x0​,y0​)=C. If its partial derivative Fy​(x0​,y0​)=0, the nearby level set is a unique continuously differentiable function graph y=g(x) through that point. The chain rule gives
Fx​(x,g(x))+Fy​(x,g(x))g′(x)=0,g′(x)=−Fy​(x,g(x))Fx​(x,g(x))​.
(7)
This proves that the local function graph solves y′=−Fx​/Fy​ there. For a different prescribed equation y′=f(x,y), one must also check Fx​+Fy​f=0 along that branch and that it stays in the domain of f. A level set by itself does not verify an arbitrary ordinary differential equation.[ref]
For F=x2+y2, the upper branch through (1,3​) has Fy​=23​ and tangent line slope −1/3​. At (2,0), however, Fy​=0 and Fx​=4. The circle remains a smooth regular level set with a vertical tangent line: it can be written locally as x=4−y2​, but not as a single function graph y=g(x) over an open interval containing 2. Moreover, −x/y is undefined there, so the scalar solution of a differential equation cannot include this point in its domain. Changing the parameter draws the curve through the point but does not extend that scalar initial value problem.
When both partial derivatives vanish, even the geometry needs separate inspection. The level x2+y2=0 is an isolated point, not a function graph on any nonempty open interval. The zero level set of G(x,y)=y2−x2 instead consists of the two lines y=x and y=−x crossing at the origin, where ∇G=0. Each line satisfies the implicit ordinary differential equation yy′=x, including at the origin; the explicit form y′=x/y excludes the origin. Thus algebraically dividing by a vanishing coefficient changes the domain and can change which solutions of a differential equation are admissible. Vanishing Fy​ alone is only failure of a sufficient test: F(x,y)=y3 has the smooth zero function graph y=0 despite Fy​=0 everywhere on it.
Implicit solutions are especially useful for exact first-order ordinary differential equations and for finding a first integral of an ordinary differential equation: a conserved relation can reveal allowed states without an explicit formula. For the normalized harmonic oscillator written as x˙=y, y˙​=−x, the energy H=(x2+y2)/2 has H˙=xx˙+yy˙​=0. Its positive level sets are the same circles. Where y=0, eliminating time gives dy/dx=−x/y and the local implicit solution above. The harmonic oscillator's parametric curve continues through y=0 because its vector field governing evolution in time is defined there; treating x as the independent variable fails at that turn. The origin is an equilibrium point of the harmonic oscillator, although it is excluded from the scalar equation y′=−x/y.

Initial value problem (u(t0​)=u0​)

Words: 431 Articles: 1
Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
An initial value problem combines an ordinary differential equation with an initial condition, for example y′=f(t,y) and y(t0​)=y0​. The task is to find a solution of a differential equation on an interval containing t0​ which has that starting value. For a continuous linear differential equation u′=A(t)u, every prescribed finite vector u0​ determines a unique solution on the coefficient interval. A boundary value problem can instead prescribe values at distinct endpoints.
For the cooling initial value problem y′=−k(y−Ta​), y(t0​)=y0​, where k>0 and Ta​ are constant, the unique solution is
y(t)=Ta​+(y0​−Ta​)e−k(t−t0​).
(8)
Take Ta​=20 degrees Celsius, y0​=80 degrees Celsius, t0​=0, and k=0.1 per minute. Then y(10)=20+60e−1≈42.07 degrees Celsius. Reaching 30 degrees Celsius requires 60e−0.1t=10, so t=10log6≈17.92 minutes. The time constant 1/k=10 minutes reduces the excess temperature by a factor e−1; it does not reduce the absolute temperature by that factor.
Uniqueness needs assumptions. If f is a continuous function on an open neighborhood of (t0​,y0​) and satisfies a local Lipschitz condition in y, uniformly in t, the Picard-Lindelöf theorem gives a unique local solution. Concretely, a finite L bounds ∣f(t,u)−f(t,v)∣≤L∣u−v∣ in a sufficiently small rectangle. Cooling satisfies this with L=k. Local existence does not promise existence for all future time: y′=y2, y(0)=1, has y(t)=1/(1−t) on (−∞,1) and finite-time blowup at t=1.
Continuity alone is insufficient for uniqueness. Consider the dimensionless initial value problem involving a square root and an absolute value:
y′=∣y∣​,y(0)=0.
(9)
Besides y(t)≡0, each delay a≥0 gives a solution for t≥0:
ya​(t)={0,(t−a)2/4,​0≤t≤a,t>a.​
(10)
At t=4, delays a=0,1,2 give y=4,9/4,1, despite identical starting data. These are valid solutions of a differential equation: for a>0, both one-sided derivatives at the join are zero; for a=0, the right derivative at the starting time is zero. After the join, ya′​=(t−a)/2=∣ya​∣​ because t>a. Squaring alone would also suggest a parabola before the join, but its negative derivative there would violate the equation. Since y′≥0, a forward solution starting from zero stays nonnegative.
The right-hand side is a continuous function but fails the Lipschitz condition at zero: for h>0, ∣∣h∣​−0∣/∣h∣=1/h​ is unbounded. Thus the Peano existence theorem still supplies local existence, while the Picard-Lindelöf theorem does not supply uniqueness. Related waiting-time examples and a sufficient uniqueness condition appear in MIT 18.034, Lecture 2: Fundamental Principles.
A brief proof outline explains the mechanism: rewrite the initial value problem as the integral equation y(t)=y0​+∫t0​t​f(s,y(s))ds. On a short enough interval, the Lipschitz condition makes the right-hand side a contraction mapping on a closed set of continuous functions near y0​. The contraction mapping theorem gives a unique fixed point; the fundamental theorem of calculus turns it back into a solution.

Degenerate ordinary differential equation

Words: 152 Articles: 1
Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A degenerate ordinary differential equation has a highest-derivative coefficient that vanishes somewhere in its domain. Its solutions can have lower regularity at that point than in the interior. A boundary value problem normally imposes endpoint values by continuous extension while requiring the differential equation in the interior. Requiring it pointwise at a degenerate endpoint with all derivatives finite can impose an extra condition and destroy existence. In a square-root-degenerate endpoint layer, the product of a vanishing square-root coefficient with a diverging second derivative has a finite nonzero interior limit.

A global continuation problem must specify its solution regularity. Across a point where a homogeneous solution vanishes to second order, its coefficient may change in a piecewise C1 continuation; requiring continuity of the second derivative can eliminate that freedom. The usual continuous-coefficient uniqueness theorem for ordinary differential equations cannot simply be applied across such a point.

∫b(y)dy​=∫a(t)dt+C.
(13)
An initial condition determines C and selects a branch and domain. The useful simplification is that the two integrals each involve only one variable, even when the original equation is nonlinear.
For Newton's law of cooling, division by y−Ta​ gives dy/(y−Ta​)=−kdt. To keep the logarithm dimensionless, integrate relative to the initial excess temperature:
log​y0​−Ta​y(t)−Ta​​​=−k(t−t0​).
(14)
When y0​=Ta​, continuity preserves the sign of the excess temperature until any potential zero, giving y−Ta​=(y0​−Ta​)e−k(t−t0​). This formula never reaches zero at finite time. Taking its derivative verifies the ordinary differential equation, and substitution at t0​ verifies the initial condition.
Always check what division removed. Each zero b(y∗​)=0 gives a constant solution of a differential equation y=y∗​. Cooling therefore also has the equilibrium point y=Ta​, omitted by division but included in the final explicit formula. For the nonunique initial value problem y′=∣y∣​, division by ∣y∣​ only describes the moving pieces: a valid solution may remain zero for an arbitrary time before joining one. Nonlinear ordinary differential equation

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A nonlinear ordinary differential equation depends nonlinearly on the unknown function or its derivatives: it cannot be written in the form defining a linear differential equation. For example, y′=y2 contains a square of the unknown function, and y′=y(1−y) is a logistic differential equation. A coefficient such as t2 depending only on the independent variable does not make an ordinary differential equation nonlinear. This distinction concerns dependence on the unknown, rather than the shape of its function graph.
For a concrete initial value problem, consider y′=y2, y(0)=y0​>0. Its solution of a differential equation is
y(t)=1−y0​ty0​​,−∞<t<y0​1​.
(15)
Taking its derivative gives y′=y02​/(1−y0​t)2=y2, and evaluating at zero checks the initial condition. The stated interval contains zero and ends at finite-time blowup: y tends to positive infinity as t approaches 1/y0​ from below. Increasing the positive initial condition brings finite-time blowup closer. This is a simple mathematical example with dimensionless t and y, rather than a calibrated physical model.
Choose y0​=1 and y0​=2, giving y1​=1/(1−t) and y2​=2/(1−2t). At t=1/4 they have values 4/3 and 4, so their sum s=y1​+y2​ has value 16/3. On the common interval 0≤t≤0.4, both are valid solutions of a differential equation, but their sum fails the same ordinary differential equation:
s′−s2=y12​+y22​−(y1​+y2​)2=−2y1​y2​=0.
(16)
Already at t=0, s=3 and its derivative is 1+4=5, whereas y′=y2 would require 9. At t=1/4, the defect s′−s2 is −32/3. The cross term explains the failure of the superposition principle, even though each individual solution of a differential equation is a smooth function.
The first panel shows y1​, y2​ and their invalid sum only up to t=0.4, before either finite-time blowup. The second measures the defect in the ordinary differential equation, including the computed value at t=1/4. For a homogeneous linear differential equation, the corresponding defect of a sum is zero. Nonlinear ordinary differential equations can describe state-dependent growth such as the logistic differential equation, whose negative quadratic term limits growth instead of accelerating it without bound. Recognizing the distinction tells us when we may assemble solutions of a differential equation from simpler pieces and when we must account for their interaction. See MIT's worked counterexample to nonlinear superposition.

Logistic differential equation (N′=rN(1−N/K))

Words: 928 Articles: 1
Nonlinear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
The logistic differential equation is the nonlinear ordinary differential equation
dtdN​=rN(1−KN​),r>0,K>0,N(0)=N0​≥0.
(17)
As a mathematical model of population dynamics, it treats abundance N as a continuous nonnegative quantity. The constant r has units of inverse time, while the carrying capacity K has the same units as N. The useful idea is to combine growth resembling exponential growth at low abundance with a slowing approach to a finite abundance. The three trajectories below already show an important distinction: starting above the carrying capacity gives a decreasing curve, whereas starting below it gives an increasing one.
For N>0, dividing the derivative by abundance gives the instantaneous per-capita rate:
NN′​=r(1−KN​).
(18)
It decreases linearly with N: it approaches r at low abundance, is r/2 at N=K/2, vanishes at the carrying capacity, and is negative above it. This per-capita rate differs from the total rate N′, which also counts how many individuals contribute. It is an instantaneous rate, rather than a fixed percentage increase over a whole day. The linear per-capita assumption and the resulting qualitative picture are developed in MIT 18.03SC's logistic-model notes.
Writing f(N)=rN(1−N/K), the equilibrium points satisfy f(N)=0, so the constant solutions of a differential equation are N(t)=0 and N(t)=K. The phase line points upward for 0<N<K and downward for N>K. Also f′(0)=r>0 and f′(K)=−r<0: the criterion for fixed point stability for an autonomous differential equation makes zero an unstable equilibrium and K an asymptotically stable equilibrium point. Every positive initial condition approaches K as t→∞; N0​=0 stays exactly zero. Instability of zero means that a small positive population grows away from it, not that a zero population spontaneously appears.
For every N0​>0, the unique solution of a differential equation for all t≥0 is
N(t)=1+(N0​K​−1)e−rtK​.
(19)
The denominator is positive on this domain, including when N0​>K. For 0<N0​<K, this is a translated and scaled logistic function; its extension to all real times is a sigmoid function. For N0​>K the coefficient of the exponential function is negative, and the future curve instead decreases toward K. No nonconstant positive solution of a differential equation crosses K or reaches it at finite time. A short derivation uses the dimensionless variable z=K/N−1: the chain rule gives z′=−rz, so exponential decay yields z(t)=(K/N0​−1)e−rt. The substitution divides by N, so the zero equilibrium point must be included separately.
The total growth rate is a downward-opening quadratic function of abundance. Completing the square gives its maximum without solving the differential equation:
f(N)=4rK​−Kr​(N−2K​)2,maxN≥0​f(N)=4rK​at N=2K​.
(20)
The balance is beautiful: more individuals contribute to growth, but each contributes less, and the strongest total increase occurs halfway to the carrying capacity. This is a maximum over possible abundances. A trajectory starting above K/2 never passes through that abundance in its future.
The chain rule connects this maximum to the shape of the time trajectory through its second derivative:
N′′=f′(N)N′=r(1−K2N​)N′.
(21)
For 0<N0​<K/2, the trajectory initially has convexity and then concavity, with its one future inflection point at
t1/2​=r1​ln(N0​K​−1),N(t1/2​)=2K​.
(22)
For N0​=K/2, this point lies at the initial time, with concavity for t>0. For K/2<N0​<K, the inflection point belongs to the past extension, so the future trajectory has concavity throughout. Above K, the decreasing trajectory has convexity and no inflection point. The two constant solutions of a differential equation have no change of concavity. Thus an entire logistic function has an S shape, but its observed future segment need not show both bends. See also [ref].
For the plotted example with K=1000, r=0.4day−1 and N0​=100, time t measured in days gives
N(t)=1+9e−0.4t1000​,N(5)≈450.85306,N(10)≈858.48645.
(23)
The initial total rate is N′(0)=0.4⋅100⋅0.9=36 individuals per day, and the initial per-capita rate is 0.36day−1. The fastest total increase is rK/4=100 individuals per day, reached at t1/2​=ln9/0.4≈5.49306 days. At that time the per-capita rate has already fallen to 0.2day−1.
These parameters are illustrative choices, rather than an empirical fit. The equation specifies deterministic evolution under a phenomenological assumption: it summarizes how net growth depends on abundance without separately modelling every process that affects it. The carrying capacity is a parameter for a specified setting, not a universal constant for all populations. In his 1838 paper "Notice sur la loi que la population suit dans son accroissement", Correspondance mathématique et physique 10, pp. 113–121, Pierre-François Verhulst proposed p′=mp−np2, equivalent to this equation with r=m and K=m/n. He also noted that different assumed growth-retarding terms could describe the observations similarly while giving very different limiting populations. This is an early illustration of why a good-looking curve alone does not establish a unique long-term prediction.[ref]
The logistic differential equation describes continuous time. Linear differential equation (L[y]=g(t))

Words: 2k Articles: 18
Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A scalar linear differential equation of order n≥1 has the form
L[y](t)=an​(t)y(n)(t)+an−1​(t)y(n−1)(t)+⋯+a1​(t)y′(t)+a0​(t)y(t)=g(t).
(35)
Here the coefficients aj​ and the forcing term g are prescribed functions of the independent variable t. A classical solution of a differential equation is an n-times differentiable function satisfying the identity at every point of its interval. The unknown function y and its derivatives enter to the first power, without products between them or coefficients depending on y. Equivalently, the differential operator L is a linear map: for constant scalars α,β,
L[αu+βv]=αL[u]+βL[v].
(36)
The forcing term may be zero, giving a homogeneous linear differential equation, or nonzero, giving an inhomogeneous linear differential equation. Linearity of L does not mean that every function graph of a solution of a differential equation is a straight line.
To use the usual order-n initial value problem theory on an interval I, assume that an​(t)=0 throughout I and that all aj​ and g are continuous functions there. Dividing by an​ normalizes the highest derivative; specifying y(t0​),y′(t0​),…,y(n−1)(t0​) at t0​∈I then selects one solution of a differential equation throughout I. A zero of an​ needs separate analysis: one cannot divide through it and retain these conclusions. The first-order normalization appears in OpenStax's definition and standard form of linear equations; the corresponding system theorem is in MIT's existence and uniqueness notes for linear systems.
The coefficients need not be linear functions of t. For example, t2y′+y=0 is a linear differential equation on t>0, although t2 is quadratic. Its solution of a differential equation with initial condition y(1)=1 is y(t)=e1/t−1: its derivative is y′=−y/t2, so substitution gives t2y′+y=0, and y(2)=e−1/2≈0.60653. The zero of the highest coefficient at t=0 explains the domain restriction. In contrast, y′+y2=0, yy′+y=0 and y′+siny=0 are nonlinear ordinary differential equations because of their dependence on the unknown function. Variable coefficients and nonlinear ordinary differential equations are different issues; see MIT's definitions and examples of first-order linear equations.
The practical benefit of linearity is that it separates the effect of the initial condition from the effect of the forcing term. Once one particular solution yp​ satisfies L[yp​]=g, every solution of a differential equation is
y=yp​+h,h∈kerL.
(37)
Here kerL is the kernel of a linear map, consisting of solutions of a differential equation to the associated homogeneous linear differential equation. Indeed, L[y−yp​]=g−g=0, and conversely L[yp​+h]=g+0=g. Thus the family for a fixed forcing term is an affine space obtained by translating kerL. If g is not identically zero, the zero function is absent, so this family is not a vector space under the usual operations on functions. This short argument explains why a general solution is a particular solution plus a homogeneous solution.

Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A Bernoulli differential equation is a first-order ordinary differential equation of the displayed form, with P and Q continuous functions on an interval and a fixed real exponent n. A nonlinear power can hide a first-order linear differential equation: on a suitable branch, the Bernoulli power substitution z=y1−n removes it exactly. The transformed solution of a differential equation can be completely regular even when recovering y produces finite-time blowup.
For example, the reciprocal Bernoulli equation with finite-time blowup y′+y=exy2 becomes z′−z=−ex under z=1/y. The initial conditions y(0)=1/2 and y(0)=−1 select a positive trajectory blowing up at x=2 and a negative trajectory tending to zero as x→∞, respectively. The integrating factor exposes both behaviors with the same short calculation.
The cases n=0 and n=1 are already first-order linear differential equations: respectively y′+Py=Q, with the zeroth-power term interpreted as the constant 1, and y′+(P−Q)y=0. There is no need for a nonlinear change of variable; for n=1, y1−n=1 would discard the unknown entirely. For other exponents, the substitution must respect the domain of exponentiation and may lose the zero solution of a differential equation.[ref]

z′=(1−n)y−ny′,y=z1/(1−n),z>0.
(70)
Multiplying the Bernoulli differential equation by (1−n)y−n yields the first-order linear differential equation
z′+(1−n)P(x)z=(1−n)Q(x).
(71)
This is an exact transformation of nonzero solutions of a differential equation on the chosen branch; it is valid far from any reference state and does not discard higher powers as a local linearization would.
Given the initial condition y(x0​)=y0​>0, the integrating factor and transformed solution of a differential equation are
μ(x)=exp((1−n)∫x0​x​P(s)ds),z(x)=μ(x)y01−n​+(1−n)∫x0​x​μ(s)Q(s)ds​.

The product rule verifies (μz)′=(1−n)μQ. Recover y=z1/(1−n) only on the connected component of {x:z(x)>0} containing x0​, inside the original coefficient interval. The first-order linear differential equation can have a longer existence interval than this inverse transformation allows.[ref]
Negative values need a separately justified real branch. For integer n, the required powers are real and differentiable for y<0 too, but the inverse must retain the sign selected by the initial condition. For n=3, z=y−2>0 represents either y=+1/z​ or y=−1/z​; both square roots are taken of positive z. For n=2, z=1/y retains the sign directly. For a general noninteger exponent, use the positive branch unless a specific differentiable real negative branch has been established. Never evaluate a real fractional power of a negative value merely because the linear formula has become negative.
Division by yn excludes y=0. When n>0 and the original real power is defined at zero, y≡0 is an additional solution of a differential equation and must be checked in the original equation. When n<0, the equation as written is undefined at zero. On a positive branch the right-hand side is locally Lipschitz in y, so the Picard-Lindelöf theorem gives local uniqueness. At zero, the same hypothesis needs a fresh check: it holds for the polynomial n=2 example, whereas for 0<n<1 a nonzero power coefficient prevents local Lipschitz continuity there. If z↓0, the inverse sends y→∞ for n>1, but sends y↓0 for 0<n<1. The latter endpoint can lead to finite-time extinction in a sublinear Bernoulli equation, where the original equation determines how to join to zero.

This second-order linear differential equation extends the Legendre differential equation by its order parameter m. Its solutions are associated Legendre functions. In a degree-one potential problem, with x=tanhη, two explicit solutions are emη(m−tanhη) and e−mη(m+tanhη). Their Wronskian with respect to η is 2m(1−m2), so the two formulas are not a fundamental pair at m=0 or m=±1.

It enters normalized spherical harmonics. Despite the traditional term associated Legendre polynomial, the factor (1−x2)m/2 is not a polynomial when m is odd. Negative integer orders satisfy Pℓ−m​=(−1)m(ℓ−m)!Pℓm​/(ℓ+m)!.

Boundedness at zero removes x−n−1, and the value at t=1 makes an​=xn. Orthogonality then gives ∫−11​G2dt=∑n​kn​x2n. The integral is x−1log((1+x)/(1−x)), so kn​=2/(2n+1). Uniform analyticity on compact subdiscs ∣x∣<1 justifies the generating expansion and termwise calculations.

Causal response of a first-order relaxation equation (G(t)=α−1e−t/αH(t))
Words: 79
First-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
For α>0, the retarded impulse response of αy′+y=f is the displayed function, with H the Heaviside step function. The corresponding convolution y(t)=α−1∫−∞t​e−(t−s)/αf(s)ds is the unique solution tending to zero in the remote past whenever the integral exists and has that limit. For example, bounded forcing that tends to zero as t→−∞ satisfies these conditions. A general forcing need not: f≡1 admits no such solution. A unit-duration pulse with α=1 gives y=0 before zero, y=1−e−t between zero and one, and y=(1−e−1)e−(t−1) thereafter.

Integrating factor (μ(t)=exp(∫t0​t​a(s)ds))

Words: 776 Articles: 3
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
An integrating factor is a nonzero multiplier that makes a differential equation directly integrable. For a first-order linear differential equation, it gathers the unknown function and its derivative into one product rule expression. Suppose a and b are continuous functions on an interval containing t0​, and consider the initial value problem
y′+a(t)y=b(t),y(t0​)=y0​.
(98)
Define A(t)=∫t0​t​a(s)ds and μ(t)=eA(t). The exact solution of a differential equation throughout that interval is
y(t)=e−A(t)[y0​+∫t0​t​eA(s)b(s)ds].
(99)
The definite integral fixes μ(t0​)=1, so the initial condition appears without an extra constant to determine. If the equation originally has a coefficient multiplying y′, first divide by that coefficient on an interval where it is nonzero; a zero of that coefficient needs separate attention. See OpenStax's first-order linear equations chapter for this normalization and the integrating factor procedure.
For a concrete balance, solve y′+2y=3 with y(0)=0. Here μ=e2t, so multiplying the entire ordinary differential equation gives (e2ty)′=3e2t. Accumulating from zero to t gives
e2ty(t)=∫0t​3e2sds=23​(e2t−1),y(t)=23​(1−e−2t).
(100)
The computed values are y(0.5)≈0.94818, y(1)≈1.29700 and y(2)≈1.47253. Its derivative is 3e−2t, which verifies y′+2y=3 exactly. Interpreting 3 as a steady input and 2y as proportional removal explains the shape: initially all input increases y, then removal catches up. The constant particular solution yp​=3/2 balances input and removal, and the homogeneous solution yh​=−23​e−2t is the transient response that corrects it to the initial condition. Because this autonomous differential equation has a time-independent right-hand side, 3/2 is also an equilibrium point.
The first panel adds the particular solution and homogeneous solution; the second shows the same balance in rates, 3=y′+2y. This links the algebra to a physical accounting rule. Newton's law of cooling has this form with a=k and b=kTa​, while an electrical circuit can have a varying input. In both cases the integrating factor systematically handles the input rather than requiring a guess for a particular solution.
Variable coefficients work just as directly. For y′+2ty=t, y(0)=0, the integrating factor is et2, and
(et2y)′=tet2,et2y(t)=21​(et2−1),y(t)=21​(1−e−t2).
(101)
Thus y(0.5)≈0.11060, y(1)≈0.31606 and y(2)≈0.49084. The derivative y′=te−t2 verifies y′+2ty=t, including at zero, where both coefficient and input vanish. No division by t is necessary. The general solution is y=1/2+Ce−t2: 1/2 is a constant particular solution, and Ce−t2 solves the associated homogeneous linear differential equation. Although this special forcing term admits a constant trajectory, this is a nonautonomous differential equation: it depends explicitly on time. Merely setting its right-hand side to zero at one instant would not establish a constant solution of a differential equation; at t=0 every state has zero slope.
The direction field shows the selected trajectory leaving its initially horizontal tangent line. For t≥0, the difference between any two solutions of a differential equation is multiplied by e−t2, rather than e−2t in the constant-rate example. This dependence on elapsed history is clearer if the exact formula is rewritten as
y(t)=y0​e−∫t0​t​a(u)du+∫t0​t​e−∫st​a(u)dub(s)ds.
(102)
For t≥t0​, each contribution from the input at s is weighted by the accumulated coefficient between s and t. The homogeneous solution remembers the initial condition; the particular solution given by the second term accumulates the forcing term with zero initial value. This decomposition differs from choosing a constant particular solution, but gives the same total. Initial-data memory tends to zero when ∫t0​t​a→+∞; a negative accumulated coefficient instead amplifies it. The reciprocal relation between integrating factor and homogeneous solution is developed in MIT's notes on solutions to linear first-order equations.
Why does the trick work? The fundamental theorem of calculus and chain rule give μ′=aμ. Consequently the product rule gives
(μy)′=μy′+μ′y=μ(y′+ay)=μb.
(103)
Integrating this identity and dividing by the positive exponential function μ produces the stated formula. Any nonzero constant multiple of μ works equally well; normalization is a convenience. This is the beauty of the method: a sum involving an unknown function becomes one exact derivative, leaving only an integral of known functions. See Oregon State's product-rule derivation. The related integrating factor for a differential one-form extends the idea of making an expression exact beyond this linear setting.
Heaviside forcing in a first-order integrating-factor equation (y(x)=μ(x)−1[μ(0)y(0)+∫0x​μ(t)H(t)dt])

Integrating factor OurBigBook.com
For y′+a(x)y=H(x) with continuous a, the integrating factor μ=exp(∫a) gives the displayed solution. It is continuous at the step and solves the differential equation classically on each side; the derivative jumps by one. The value assigned to the Heaviside step function at the single point zero does not affect the integral. A discontinuity in y would instead produce an unintended delta term in its distributional derivative.
Integrating factor for a differential one-form (∂x​(μf)=∂y​(μg))

Integrating factor OurBigBook.com
For the differential one-form fdy+gdx, a nonzero integrating factor μ makes μfdy+μgdx an exact differential form locally. If it equals dF, then Fy​=μf, Fx​=μg, and equality of mixed partial derivatives gives the displayed compatibility condition. Conversely this condition is local sufficiency for smooth coefficients on a small rectangle; global exactness additionally depends on the domain. Zeros of the multiplying factor can change the solution set, so equivalence is asserted only where the factor is nonzero.
